blocks.x: You know, like I just want to know your real name, your right name.
Dick, there is a little bit of a hum.
Yes. Let me listen to it. It may be the air conditioner. Maybe we could shut this door, huh? Just to, uh...
Okay. Alright.
Go. So, I was going to ask you your real name.
My real name is Jeff. It's not Jefferson. It's just Jeff. Sullivan. Because me mother was a Sullivan.
I see.
Riddick. R-I-D-D-I-C-K. Senior.
I see. Is it picking my voice up? Oh, good. Then I can tell my name. Dick Allen. I guess you should tell yours if it picks you up.
I don't know if it picks me up. Yes, it does. Yeah. Oh, this is Pam Tyler.
Okay. Good. Well, it seems, everything seems to be working. Good.
Please excuse me.
That's alright. Don't worry about it.
You can cut that out anyway.
Oh, sure.
Yeah.
Well. I thought I'd ask you about when you were born and where to start with.
I was born in Oakland, Mississippi. Which is about 65 miles south of Memphis.
Mm-hmm.
On the IC Railroad. June 3rd, 1907.
Mm-hmm. And were you from a musical family at all?
You said your mother? Oh, yes. My mother was a concert pianist. My father played breakdown fiddle, hoedown fiddle, if you want to call it that. Country fiddle.
Mm-hmm.

And all of my brothers played. There were four boys and we all four played. My oldest brother, Tom, never did become a professional pianist. He played nice piano, but he couldn't keep time with an eight-day alarm clock.
You've said that before. Yeah.

My next oldest brother, Johnny, Johnny Riddick, played piano in one of the finest Dixieland jazz bands in the 20s. He was six years in the Arcadia Ballroom in St. Louis. He was with the Arcadian Serenaders. The original name of the band was the Crescent City Jazzers. They originated in Mobile, Gulfport, and New Orleans. Wingy Munoon was one of the first trumpet players in that band. And Harry Tolson was one of the first clarinet players in that band, but he left that band pretty soon. And he was replaced by Cliff Holman, originally from Birmingham, Alabama. The drummer in the band just died just two years ago. Felix Guerrino, he was the original drummer in the band. He died at the age of 84 years old in Mobile. And he was originally a New Orleans boy.
I didn't know that. That somehow slipped my attention.

My brother Johnny was also born in Oakland, Mississippi. Just exactly what year. I think it was 1903. My oldest brother Tom was born in 1900. Then the next oldest brother, Dick, his name was Richard, was in 1929, acclaimed the world's greatest harmonica player in Berlin, Germany, at the Hohner harmonica factory. He had the honor of playing in the presence of President von Hindenburg in Germany in that contest. And he won that acclaim. We were both with Bora Menovic harmonica band in 1928. And we were with Helen Kane in Good Boy, the Boop Boop Be Doop Girl. Now, after that, I went to school, Spring Hill College in Mobile one year. Finished in business administration in LSU. Met my wife in April 1931 and married her in August 1931. We're still together. 52 years this coming August.
Congratulations.
Congratulations, indeed.
You can look at that beautiful plaque up there on the wall. It's by my niece. Her daughter made that. They are in the trophy business in Mobile, Alabama. Isn't that nice? That is. Yeah.
Back up to Mississippi. Were there any bands around Oakland or Jossman or Tempo?

No. No. No. Just, I'll tell you what. They used to have bands to come in. Now, for instance, I sat on W.C. Handy Handy's knee when I was a little bitty fella. And he and my father were personal friends. Handy, of course, was from Memphis. And it was from Handy that I learned all of the St. Louis blues and the Memphis blues. And I can tell you an instance. When I was playing with Sharky, someone asked for the Memphis blues. And no one in the band knew anything about the Memphis blues but the last part of it. Da-da-da, da-da-da-da-da-da, da-da-da-da, da-da-da-da, da-da-da-da, da-da-da-da. But actually, there are three parts to it. And I knew it, but I couldn't bring it in that very night. But let me tell you what happened. The very next afternoon when I went to take my nap, before I went to work at the famous door, I dreamed that I was a child sitting on Handy's knee while he played all of the Memphis blues. And I went to work that night and played it. That's funny. May God strike me dead if that's not the truth. Now, what else you want to know?
Did you ever get around Tippo, Mississippi?
Good Lord. It would have been on Tippo and Sumner and Webb and all of those towns up there. Well, you fished in the Sunflower River and the Yollabusha River, Tallahatchie River, all of that country.
Yeah. But you know, Moe's Allison Sr. had the story.
Oh, yes. But I never had the pleasure of meeting him. No. But he was one fine piano man. Mm-hmm.
Well, the father, too. And I talked to his father once. I was passing up that way, going my way to Memphis, and I stopped off. And I just wondered if you knew him.
Never had the pleasure. I was sorry that I never, because he was one fine piano man. And he's just a good old country boy.
Yeah.
They say that he came from so far back out in the country that the sun set between his house and town. But how long did you stay in Oakland? One year.
Only one year?
Yeah. That was when I was a baby.
Mm-hmm.

Then my family moved to Charleston, Mississippi, just 10 miles away. And that's where I was raised until I was 12 years old. And my father owned a big commissary store, like, handled everything. They called it a commissary. Groceries, dry goods, suits, clothing, shirts, socks, underwear, everything under the sun. And he also, I was raised in an 11-room beautiful home. And he had five other houses. My father also was a cotton broker. And that was just during the war that the prices of cotton went up from 10 cents a pound to a dollar a pound. And with the idea that it was going to raise up to a dollar and a half a pound, my father mortgaged everything in the world that he had and bought 7,000 bales of cotton, each one weighing an average of 500 pounds a bale. With the prospect of it going up to a dollar and a half a pound, which would have made him $350,000.
But it didn't go up.
It didn't go up. The crash came.
Mm-hmm.

And the bottom dropped out of it, and he lost everything that he had, including our homes and everything. All right. At that very time, my mother died at the age of 39 years old. Broke my father's heart. He got sick and almost died himself. Doctor told him there wasn't one thing in the world that would save him. He wanted to change climates and locations and everything and get away from the whole thing. And at the same time, in his store, he had a woman that was a cashier there in his store who was a very, very fine person. And she was a willer. My father and that lady, whom I loved with all my heart, were married. And they were married 29 years when my father died. But they bought a 20-acre truck farm in Long Beach, Mississippi. And we came down to the Gulf Coast. That was right after that that my brother went with the Crescent City Jazzers, don't you see?
Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.
Avery Lopasa, the trombone player, was a golf board boy.
Mm-hmm.
And he had heard my brother Johnny play.
And you knew Eddie Powers, too.
Very well.
He was another one in there.
And Sock Horn, Sterling Bowes, after William Manone left the band, Sterling Bowes joined that band.

I've got the picture. I can show you the picture of that band. Who's that? Sock? What did you say his name? Sock Horn. What did he play? Sax. Great, big, powerful man. Mm-hmm. I'm just not familiar with him. Where is he from?
From, I don't know. Mm-hmm. I think it was Mobile.
Mm-hmm.
Could have been easily, sure. Did you go over there to Mobile much and hear the band?

Oh, yes. Fairhope? Oh, that was the first. Fairhope, the old Point Clear Hotel in Fairhope was the first piano job that I had in my life. And I played at the Point Clear Hotel in Fairhope. That was in 1926. I played drums five years before. Almost five years. How I began to play drums was the fact that some, they were organizing a little band in Long Beach where I was living and going to school, going to high school. And a drummer, not a drummer, a guy bought a set of drums to play in the band and he couldn't play to save his life. He played waltz time backwards. Instead of playing dah, he played dah, It was like a sign.
Isn't that beautiful?

So one night, he says, anybody that can catch these GD sticks when I throw them up in the air can have my set of drums. When he threw them up in the air, I caught both of them, and I played drums from that time on because I was born to keep time with music. Don't you see? Keep the beat. And one night, Roger Johnson got a heart attack in the Dukes, and I saved the night. I played drums with the Dukes of Dixieland, with their original Dukes, you know, their Santo boys.
That's incredible. It came right back to you, enough to keep the beat going?
It never does leave you. If it's there originally, if you're born with it, it never leaves you. Now you may be rusty at it. But all it needed was somebody to keep time.
Well, how much older were you than Dick?
Who? Your brother, Dick. I was the youngest. You were the youngest? Yeah. Dick was almost three years older than I.
I see. So, when you played drums, was it strictly with your school chums, or your family, or everybody?

No! With the bands all over the coast. I was in the first band that ever played in the Markham Hotel, in Gulfport. I played in the Buena Vista, played in the Markham. I played in Paris Christiane, at Henderson Point, how you had to take the ferry. That was before they had that bridge across. stuff
Bay St. Louis, you know, at Hennison Point. I forget the name of the old Reese Hotel, if I remember. Reed, Reed, R-E-E-D.
What did you all wear when you played? Did you all have to dress up?
Tux. Everything was tux in those days. Backwing collar.
Yeah.
And I've hated them until this very day, and I wouldn't buy one of them right now if I never got another job. I've got a dozen nice soft collar tux shirts.
Anyway, were these solo jobs or with bands?
Bands. Seven piece bands. Six and seven piece bands.
Whose bands were they, though?
It's the hardest thing in the world to answer that one because there were no leader prices and all. You wouldn't say that there's any. We just all got together. That was all.
Would there be anybody that I'd ever heard of?
No.
Do you remember any of the names?
Oh, yes. The Munch brothers. Eddie Dubazon was a barber. He played trombone. Dick Mackey.
Oh, yes.

I know him. Would come over and play jobs with us all the way from New Orleans. Well, it only cost you about $1.35 to come from New Orleans to Long Beach or Gulfport on a train. And that was the first time that I ever played with Dick Mackey. I played drums in that band. The first time I ever played with Tony Almerico was at the Dog Track in Biloxi. That was 1923. And I played drums in that band.
My goodness. Was Dick Mackey a good corner player there?
Oh, Dick showed them all how. Dick equaled Emmett Hardy. Dick was just fine. And his brother, his brother, Red Mackey played bass.
Mm-hmm.

And Red and Dick both were playing in the Owls. And they used to come from New Orleans and go to DeLille and play dances. They had a pavilion there, a big dance pavilion. There was dance there every Saturday night. And they had a pretty fairly well-named band to play those dances. And it just packed.
Would you say that Dick sounded anything like a...

Dick sounded like all of them. Sounded like George Girard. Dick sounded like Sterling Bowes. Dick sounded like anybody that played good. Oh, yeah. There was never a bad note Dick ever played that I know of.
Yeah.
I've got a picture of him when he was a very young man.
He certainly... It was a tragedy that he had to stop playing. That was awful. See, I never got to hear him at all. Oh, he was just great.

Just great. Beautiful tone out of a horn. Mm-hmm. He got a tone. He played sort of like Sharky did. All those years... Well, I would say that Sharky and Dick both almost grew up together. You would saw practically. Except Dick was from a very fine family.
Mm-hmm.
Period. Period.
Who were the Munch brothers? What were their names? Oh, well. If it didn't come to you, don't worry about it.
I'd have to remember.
And Tony Almerico was playing in 1923.
Oh, yes, sir.
Was he old then?
No. I mean, how old? Was he just a kid? Of course he wasn't. He was just...
No, he couldn't have been.
He wasn't, but about 21 years old himself. And he... Excuse me.
You were even younger than that.
Oh, yes.
You were really a kid.
Oh, yes.
Were you still in school at the time you played? Yeah.
I played my way through school.
Did they have bands around Spring Hill College? Did you have a college band?

Oh, yes. The first band that I played with in Mobile, the trumpet player was Joe Walsh. Joe Walsh and I went to Spring Hill together. He was, without a doubt, the most superstitious person that you ever saw in your life. And when we'd go to Fairhope, we'd play on the ferry all the way from Mobile to Fairhope across Mobile Bay. And that's the way we got over there, by playing. We got transportation. Then we'd go and play at the casino for the Funk Brothers at Fairhope. And then that was in the afternoon. Then that night, we would go and play at Point Claire Hotel. All right. The trumpet player in the band was Joe Walsh. Now, Joe Walsh, after he finished university, became a priest. Joe Walsh was Father Joe Walsh at Loyola University, was Spanish, the dean of Spanish, there for many, many years. He's back in Mobile, completely retired now. All right. He was the trumpet player. Clarinet player was Bobby Swartz, an absolute nervous wreck, and I think that he has passed away. But he played fine clarinet. We had a banjo player named Ed Vaughn. We called him Putt. Putt was one of the finest men that I ever met, and he is president of some big lumber company in New York State now. He was in my home and had dinner with me not too long. We've never forgotten each other, and then the love we had for each other, the friendship. The drummer we had in the band was Eddie Jones. He was one of the funniest fellas I ever met in my life, and he played drums until all of a sudden he just dropped in. Dr. David Fridge played tenor in the band. We didn't have a trombone player. There weren't any at that time.
Did Fridge come over here?
No. Fridge died about five years ago in Mobile. He was a dentist.
I've heard of him. I just wondered where I'd heard of him. I think Johnny Hyman or whatever you want to call him mentioned him.

They knew each other. Johnny knew him very well because he mentioned him many times. I knew Johnny Hyman since 1926. Johnny Wiggs. That's Johnny Wiggs. Same person. The name you've seen him, right? He said something mighty nice for me the last time I ever heard of him, and this was in the second line. The last write-up that he got. I don't know if you saw it, but anyway, he was talking about the different musicians that he'd played with, and when he got down to me, he said, oh, Professor Jeff Riddick, the old parson, words to that effect, he said, he's the finest orchestra man in the city of New Orleans, and I'll never forget that. Of course, he liked you very much. He loved me, and I loved him because we were such good friends, but he was dead and buried before I knew it. No one called me.
There was no, there was a private service, you know. Yeah. His family was strange about that. They didn't want anybody to know.
They let Raymond know. They called Raymond. They called Raymond. Well, you know Raymond. Raymond will sit on his fat end, never tell anybody anything at no time. That's Raymond.
Who was Raymond?
Raymond Burke.

He's too shy to make a phone call. He played with his brother. I was talking about when I was so nervous before getting married, I didn't know what to do. I couldn't find anybody to talk to, so I called up his brother, and we talked about Raymond. Raymond played over there, I guess in Faro with him.

Oh, yes. Raymond and I first met at the Edgewater Gulf, and Raymond was playing at the Midway Inn, and I was playing with Johnny Batusi, Toots Batusi, the old man, at the Midway at another time, and Raymond came over and played some spot jobs at the Edgewater Gulf with some fiddle player. I don't quite remember his name.
I'll have to ask Raymond about that.
Raymond will tell you.
Yeah.
Raymond's older than I am. Raymond would remember better than I.
Well, he's...
Raymond's almost 80 years old. Yeah. Saw him the other day. Oh, yeah.
I run into him and his buddy Gaston Olivier. They were all...
Yeah, yeah, they were together. Yeah.
Hunting for junk.
Oh, yeah, and I was playing at the gazebo at the time.
Oh, yeah.
That was the eight hours that I played at the gazebo, and Raymond came by and said hello.
That's right. All the foreign musicians are using you now. You're playing with all the foreigners now. Sure. You told me it was...
And they're more fun.
Really?
Yes. They're more white than most of the other musicians that you play with in New Orleans.

That's... You mean in the sense of playing like white musicians or in the sense of... Oh, sure. Yeah. Well, I think they're getting around to appreciating people. Fusier Wright was responsible for a lot of that somehow. They began to appreciate him. He was the one that they sort of fell in love with.
Well, Tony?
Tony, yeah.

Tony and I were playing five years together before Ellen and I, my wife, met. And Tony was my best man at my wedding. Oh, yeah. We were married in Ellen's house and Tony lived one block from my wife. And Tony and I, I was one of Tony's pallbearers. And I still take Margie to the doctor. Oh, yeah? And she needs me to. I always take Margie and I always will until the day either one of us dies. Margie's 80, over 80. About 82 now. Almost totally blind. And she had to have me because I, you know, got a pretty strong arm and could take her, you know, and take care of her. She and Gloria and I, that's their oldest daughter, would take her to the doctor.
I can't remember Gloria. I remember Patsy.
Yeah.

But I get them confused. But we were there together. You know what you said when they were passing the sensor around with all the smoke coming out of it? What? I don't know if we should put this on tape of the other. Go ahead. But you said if it had been grass, Tony would have gotten up in smoke smoke.
Well, I would too.
You see, There is no generation gap.
If you want to get it, if you want to talk a little bit about smoking grass, those days was, it's so different than it is today that it's pitiful. It was a sin to smoke grass when I smoked grass.
Mm-hmm.
So nobody hardly ever did but just us.
Mm-hmm.

Today, it's the most public thing in the world. I have seen doctors go out and puff it with musicians. I know. I know good and well. I don't do it anymore, but I'm fooled with it because it's no good anymore.
Well, where did you get it? Way back when you were a young musician and used to smoke it. Where would you...

You could go on St. Philip Street in the 500 block and you go into the men's room. Uh-huh. And there was a little hole in the wall about that big and another little hole in the wall. You knocked on the wall. A finger went through the hole. You put your finger in the hole for the size of the stick that you wanted. If you bought a single, it was 15 cents. If you bought a... They called it... Let me see. What did they call it? A double, I believe. It was 20 cents. And it was three times as big as these that you pay $2 for a day. and that this today is absolutely no good because they never do wait until it matures to pick it. And there wasn't ever known at that time for it to ever be grown anywhere in the United States that I ever heard of. It was all strictly Mexican. Not even Colombia.
Well, it wasn't illegal.

Oh, yes it was. Then? Yes. As far as... If anyone was ever caught, I don't know of anybody ever going to jail with it on account of it. But all you had to do was go down to St. Philip Street and knock on the wall and stick your finger in the hole for the... and 20 cents was all you could afford in those days. So it was... The first piano job that I had when I left Mobile and came to New Orleans was at the Silver Slipper and that was with a little small push-around piano, short keyboard about that big and I played... It was during Prohibition and I played for girls singers to go around to push around tables during intermission. Merritt Brunis had the band there. Henry Brunis played trombone in the band. Bullfellow played piano from Biloxi.

Buck Rogers played drums. Red, I can't remember his last name from Biloxi, played sax. Not Parks Wilkes now, Parks Wilkes played over on the Gulf Coast with Ellis Stratikas. That was where I first knew Ellis Stratikas was on the coast. That was before Ellis Stratikas came to New Orleans to play.
When did you come to New Orleans first?
1926, then I left and went back to school.
You were a youngster then?
Oh yeah, 19 years old, 1926.
And when did you go to Spring Hill?
Went on back to Spring Hill almost. I was only here in New Orleans just a year, then I went to Spring Hill.
That would have been around 27?
27. And then you went on to LSU?

Left there, after finishing there I got a job with a band in Baton Rouge playing in a restaurant. And we were playing spot jobs in Baton Rouge with Mutt Powers and Fliver Ford and Tony Fougerat. Oh yeah?
Fliver Ford. That's a great name, Fliver Ford. Yeah, Fliver Ford.
His name was, his real name you would never guess was Jewel.
Well, Fliver was better.

Yeah. So everybody called him Fliver. One of the funniest characters that I ever knew in my life. He was a constant laugh. Died very young, dropped dead. J.B. Landry was in the band. Freddie, some played banjo.
What did Fliver Ford play?
One instrument? Fliver played guitar and banjo. Freddie, whatever his name, I can't remember his name, saved my life. He was the original banjo player in that band. Then Fliver Ford took his place.
Well I'm getting confused on who played what instrument. Is it J.B.
Landry? J.B. Landry played alto sax. Tony Fougerat played trumpet. Mutt Powers played drums. Fliver Ford played banjo and I played piano. And that was the band.
Oh, they're on that phonograph? Uh huh.
Those are my two granddaughters. And that's my youngest son there. That's when he graduated from De La Salle High School. He's graduated already from New Orleans University.
What's his name?
Ted.
That's Ted.
Okay, and you have a... He's a paramedic in the New Orleans Fire Department. Uh huh. Been there nearly eight years now. Uh huh. Got a fine job at the New Orleans Fire Department.
Well back to Baton Rouge, we're gonna get to your wife. You said she was a dancer when the machine was off.
All right. Uh huh. Tony Fougerat, Mutt Powers, Fliver Ford, and J.B. Landry and myself were playing across the river in Plaquemine in a professional gambling place. And I mean big stakes too.
Uh huh.

Uh huh. Dewey Luke, Cy Million, all of those fellas banked this Alfred Hirsch, one of the most prominent men in that part of the country. Uh huh. And very rich, a multi-millionaire owned the Tivoli Club. Uh huh. And we were the first band that played there. In about five months or something like that, we got this offer to go on the road with this unit that was leaving the Sanger Theater for the summer. In that unit was six girls in a line. It was no burlesque or nothing like that. It was just strictly a tab, skits and things like that, you know, with comedians and things like that. And Ellen was dancing in that line. And we fell in love in April and married in August and we've been together ever since and we've, thank God I've got sense enough to every time I make a paycheck bring it home and give it to her. And we've gotten along just marvelously well and today I'm totally independent, thank God. And it's a mighty, mighty good feeling. And it's 76, I don't know, five cents. This home is worth $150,000 and it's, I can get that for it. This one right here just sold for $98,000.
You had all sons?
We had three sons and lost the middle one. He didn't live but 23 hours. He was born with bronchopneumonia and died.
Well, the first one would have been, what's his name?
Jeff Junior. Jeff Junior.
And when was he born? 1938.
Jeff will be 47 years old. No, No, Jeff will be 45 years old this 10th of November.
And then, who were you playing with when Jeff was born? I'm just trying to set up some dates in my mind if you can remember.

Dutch Andrus. Steve Massico. Sherwood Man Japan. Me on piano. Al Moore on trombone. And Steve Boudreau on drums. Just learned of his death not too long ago. In Baker, Oregon. Steve Boudreau. I taught him how to play drums. He had the natural gift and I just taught him how to keep time and from there he went on by himself. And they are the jazz players that really play the swing. They're the natural gifted ones.
Well, did any musicians help you when you were learning? Yeah.
They played good. And that helped you. That helped me.
Yeah. But they never sat down with a pair of drums and showed you anything?

Not one part of them, no. I wouldn't know of, I don't even know the, what do you call it, parabellum or something? Paradiddle. Diddle, paradiddle. I wouldn't know of paradiddle from a monkey doodle, from a Yankee doodle. Yeah.
And with the piano, did anybody show you chords or anything?
No.
They didn't help you at all? No.
Everything?
I went and bought the books and taught myself. So you did have some teaching but through books? Through experience and learning.

Yeah. And just got the books, I got chord construction, chord construction and analysis by Gibbs. And I just started from there. And then I had some wonderful experience for five years with Paul Jacobs. Paul Jacobs was nine years in the San Carlos Opera Company. And I played accompaniment for him when he taught singing. Mm-hmm. I had to learn through Paul Jacobs to, to transpose and play in all different keys on the same tune. And I had to drop a half a step by just the sign that he gave me without saying a word. If he, if he turned his finger down and put it right like that, a half an inch, it meant to drop a half a step. Or if he did this, it meant to raise it a half a step. Or if he did that, it meant to raise it one step completely. And then I had to do it without even losing the lead on the melody. That was to suit that particular voice.
Well, so you, but you did pick up reading then of course, that you did that to an extent.
I couldn't read a note. But you, you figured out the chords. But I just, I just listened to thousands of tunes. Yeah, I see. And stayed with the popular hit tunes.
Mm-hmm. I just wondered how you'd pick up the things out of the, out of the book without being able to read. Must have been able to spell, as they say. I said, I know.
He gave me two or three tunes at a time and said, take these home and woodshed them.
Mm-hmm.

And I'd get on and sit on and figure it out and figure it all out. And now if I showed you how I have learned to play the one lead, one line, you understand? Yeah. On mass and all that kind of stuff. I've worked it out to where I can almost sit on and at sight now and read the one line. Mm-hmm. Because I've got thousands and thousands of tunes in the sheet music. Yeah. And I play thousands of tunes because I don't let them leave me by the titles. You understand? I sit down and I may take five different books with titles of tunes. If you wait just a second I'll get one of them and I'll be right back.
Yeah.
Turn it off. All the way there.
That's just a little nice. Mm-hmm. The red light's on. Let's take that. Okay. So you've got one of your books here.
So I've got a book here. In other words, these are the titles to songs. All of these that you see with the little dots on them are tunes that I know.
Now you've got an X by All Through the Night.
That means to learn that one. I'm stumbling a little bit on it.
Yeah. What's closest to pages in a book? That's a different song.
Well, Jim Garrison called me one day. Jim and I are personal friends. We were personal friends before he ever ran for the first office.
Yeah.

And I helped by just talking for him. Jim used to come to the red carpet. Joe Wright owned the red carpet club. That was where I first met Jim. And Jim called me not too long ago and asked me, he says, he's divorced from his wife. He says, I am in love with a girl that I have known since I was a little fellow. And he says, her favorite is close as pages in a book. All right. He says, do you know that? I said, no. But let me look and I'll see. Jim was almost ready to go on his bench. Well, Jim was almost ready to go on his bench. He's a judge. So, I looked it up and it's in this book. Closest pages in a book. And he wanted the words to the tune. I called his secretary and told, gave her the words and she copied them down and gave them to Jim. Now, where I first met Jim was he fell in love with me because he says, do you know an old tune called, you're the cream in my coffee? You're the cream in my coffee. Da Yeah. And I knew it. And he just, we've been just personal friends ever since then. And this is only one book. You see, it's just. Oh yeah. I know all of these tunes that you see with a pencil mark on them. So you. I can play any one of them you ask me for.
That's nearly all of it out of a thousand in this book, I guess.
Yeah, that's just one book.
That's one thousand. But it's incredible to me. And that, I guess that's the only one where you have that sort of upside down check mark, closest pages in the book.
Yeah.
But the majority of them. Let's show it to Pam to give her some idea of how many you know. The large majority, nearly all of those he knows. Out of a thousand too. Yeah, nearly every one.
